Medicines law, exemptions, product licences and guidance change: always check the current BNF, the College's Clinical Management Guidelines and your lecturer's slides before relying on a dose or legal detail.

topics.title: How eye drops reach their target
topics.summary: Only a small fraction of an eye drop gets into the eye. Most overflows or drains down the nasolacrimal duct, where it can be absorbed into the blood. To cross the cornea a drug needs to dissolve in both fats (to pass the epithelium) and water (to pass the stroma). Understanding this explains dosing, side effects and why technique matters.
keyPoints: A typical drop is about 30–50 µl, but the eye holds only about 7–10 µl, so most of it is lost straight away.
Drainage through the nasolacrimal duct lets drugs reach the bloodstream through the nasal lining, bypassing the liver: this is how eye drops cause systemic side effects.
The corneal epithelium is lipophilic (fat-loving) and the stroma hydrophilic (water-loving), so the best drugs have both properties.
Closing the eyes or pressing on the inner corner (punctal occlusion) for 1–2 minutes increases absorption into the eye and reduces systemic absorption.
Darker irides bind some drugs to melanin, so dilation can be slower and sometimes needs more drops.
Preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride keep multi-dose bottles sterile but can damage the ocular surface with long-term use.
examTraps: Assuming eye drops can't cause systemic effects: timolol drops can cause bronchospasm.
Giving two different drops one immediately after the other: the second washes out the first; wait about 5 minutes.
Forgetting that a damaged epithelium lets drugs (and toxicity) in much more easily.

diagram.description: A drop landing on the eye, with arrows showing: overflow onto the cheek, drainage through the punctum and nasolacrimal duct to the nose and bloodstream, and a small arrow passing through the cornea (epithelium, stroma, endothelium) into the anterior chamber. Add a finger pressing the inner corner to show punctal occlusion.

goDeeper.heading: Getting drops in well
goDeeper.body: Tilt the head back, pull the lower lid down, look up and put one drop into the pocket without touching the eye or lashes. Close the eye gently for 1–2 minutes (don't blink hard) and press the inner corner. Wait about 5 minutes between different drops, and put ointments in last. Many patients, especially older ones, struggle with technique, so show them and consider aids.

goDeeper.heading: Formulations
goDeeper.body: Solutions are quick but short-acting. Suspensions (for example some steroids) need shaking. Gels and ointments stay longer and are useful at night but blur vision. Preservative-free single-use vials suit patients using drops often, those with surface disease, and contact lens wearers. Pro-drugs (such as latanoprost) are changed into the active form inside the eye.

goDeeper.heading: Systemic absorption
goDeeper.body: Drug absorbed through the nose goes straight into the circulation without first passing through the liver. That's why a beta-blocker drop can slow the heart or tighten the airways, and why cyclopentolate can occasionally cause behaviour changes in small children. Punctal occlusion and using the lowest effective strength reduce the risk.

topics.title: Selecting and using diagnostic drugs safely
topics.summary: From Dr Bhogal-Bhamra's week 9 lecture: only use diagnostic drops within your competence and after the right checks. Explain, ask about past reactions, get consent, do the 4D check, check the angle and IOP around dilation, take care with cycloplegics and anaesthetics, and record everything.
keyPoints: Before any drop: explain why, what it will do and when it wears off; ask about previous problems or reactions; get consent (or assent). Warn first-timers about possible effects.
4D check at the patient's shoulder: Drug (the right one), Dose, Date (in date), Dispose (can you dispose of it properly).
Record the drug, concentration, number of drops, which eye, batch number, expiry and all advice given.
Dilation: tropicamide is the drug of choice; add phenylephrine for more profound dilation. Angle closure risk is about 1 in 5,000.
Before dilating: check the angle (van Herick, gonioscopy, shadow test or AS-OCT), IOP and symptoms of sub-acute angle closure. After: angles and IOP again. Don't dilate with an iris-clip lens.
Advise sunglasses and no driving, cycling or machinery until vision recovers; refer suspected angle closure to eye casualty as an emergency and tell the GP.

Cycloplegia: cyclopentolate is the drug of choice, usually for children (angle and IOP checks are hard; check them in young adults). Record VA and a dry refraction first, watch for reactions, and recheck vision with the result after it wears off (24–48 hours), making sure they're not fogged.
Topical anaesthetics: no specific pre-tests, but ask about past reactions; they're potentially highly toxic, so always check for staining afterwards.
examTraps: Skipping post-dilation IOP and angle checks.
Forgetting to record batch number and expiry.
Dilating a patient with an iris-clip lens.

diagram.description: An iris showing the circular sphincter (parasympathetic, muscarinic receptors) and the radial dilator (sympathetic, alpha-1 receptors). Arrows show tropicamide and cyclopentolate blocking the sphincter and ciliary muscle, and phenylephrine stimulating the dilator.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: drug timings
goDeeper.body: Tropicamide 0.5–1% works in about 20–30 minutes and lasts around 4–6 hours with mild cycloplegia. Phenylephrine 2.5% is an alpha-1 agonist; take care with heart disease and high blood pressure. Cyclopentolate 0.5% under about 1 year, 1% in older children, peaking at 30–60 minutes. Anaesthetics work in seconds and last about 15–20 minutes. Fluorescein shows epithelial loss and is used for TBUT, Goldmann tonometry and the Seidel test.

checklist.title: Safe routine dilation
steps: Check history: previous dilation, heart problems, high blood pressure, medicines (for example MAOIs), allergies and pregnancy.
Assess the angle (Van Herick) and note risk factors for angle closure (hyperopia, older age, narrow angles).
Explain the purpose, effects (blur, glare) and that they shouldn't drive until vision recovers; get verbal consent.
Check the drug name, strength, expiry date and that the container is intact.
Instil the drop(s) and record drug, strength, number of drops, eye, time and batch number.
Re-check pupils and IOP if indicated after examination, and give written advice about warning symptoms (pain, redness, haloes).
Tell the patient to seek urgent help if they get a painful red eye or headache with haloes.

cases.scenario: A 58-year-old with a history of heart disease is booked for routine dilation to examine diabetic retinopathy. His angles are open (Van Herick grade 3).
cases.question: Which drops would you use and what advice would you give?
cases.modelAnswer: Tropicamide alone (for example 1%) is usually enough and avoids the cardiovascular risk of phenylephrine. Explain blur and glare, advise him not to drive until his vision recovers, and tell him to seek urgent help for a painful red eye, haloes or headache. Record drug, strength, time and batch.

topics.title: Adverse drug reactions and reporting
topics.summary: From the week 11 and 12 PaP lectures: what adverse reactions are and how they're classified, the optometrist's role in monitoring, detecting and reporting them via the Yellow Card scheme, and the reactions to know for the topical diagnostic drugs.
keyPoints: Adverse reaction: an unintended harmful effect of a correctly given drug. Side effect: a secondary unwanted effect. Allergic reaction: an immune response, an emergency. OAR: an ocular adverse reaction.
Types A and B, plus C (continuing), D (delayed) and E (end-of-use).
Optometrists see many patients regularly across all ages, so they can monitor, detect (with baseline data) and report. Reporting implies no criticism and the medication usually continues.

Report suspected reactions on a Yellow Card (MHRA or BNF) and inform the GP; emergency referral isn't usually needed. Report all suspected reactions to black-triangle drugs, and serious ones to established, OTC and herbal products, with extra care for under-18s and the elderly. Device incidents (e.g. contact lenses) are reportable too.
Likelihood depends on the drug (dose, nature, interactions), the patient (age, with reactions peaking about 70; history; genetics) and their condition (chronic disease, metabolism).
Tropicamide: dry mouth, tachycardia, headache, nausea, pallor, allergy; the sight-threatening risk is acute angle closure (severe pain, redness, haloes, headache, vomiting, corneal oedema).

Cyclopentolate 1%: systemic effects in up to 10% after repeated doses (tachycardia, restlessness, hallucinations, ataxia, seizures). Atropine poisoning: dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, hot dry flushed skin, fast pulse; seek emergency advice.

Topical anaesthetics: stinging and redness most common; the major ocular reaction is corneal desquamation (VA can drop to about 6/60). Avoid repeat doses and rubbing; no contact lenses for 25 minutes.
Chloramphenicol: rare aplastic anaemia and other systemic reactions; avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and neonates (grey baby syndrome).
examTraps: Thinking a Yellow Card means stopping the drug or criticising the prescriber: it doesn't.
Only reporting serious reactions for black-triangle drugs: report all suspected ones.
Giving patients anaesthetic drops to take home.

topics.title: Medicines law for optometrists
topics.summary: From the week 10 PaP lecture: the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 control medicines, enforced by the MHRA. Know the POM, P and GSL categories, signed orders, medical devices, and the four levels at which optometrists can use, supply and prescribe.
keyPoints: The Human Medicines Regulations 2012 replaced the Medicines Act 1968; the MHRA enforces them through the Commission on Human Medicines. Medicines are normally supplied from registered pharmacies.

POM (about 4,500): only on a prescription from an appropriate practitioner, from a pharmacy. P (about 1,200): any medicine not on the other lists, sold under a pharmacist. GSL (about 1,500): any secure shop; for optometrists mainly eye lotions (eye drops and ointments aren't GSL).
A drug can fall into more than one category depending on pack size, strength and use (e.g. sodium cromoglicate).
Signed orders (needed for entry-level and AS drugs): your name, address and GOC number, date, patient details if relevant, drug, quantity, form and strength, labelling and your original signature.

Medical devices are separately regulated but adverse events still go to the MHRA: contact lenses and solutions are class IIb, fluorescein strips class I. Controlled drugs (Misuse of Drugs Act 1971) don't apply to optometric practice.

Four levels: entry (registration) level, additional supply, supplementary prescribing, independent prescribing. AS, SP and IP need GOC-approved training (a postgraduate course and supervised hospital placement).

Entry level P medicines include antazoline, chloramphenicol 0.5% (acute bacterial conjunctivitis), propamidine, sodium cromoglicate, lodoxamide, phenylephrine, naphazoline, fluorescein, rose bengal and tear substitutes.

AS covers non-sight-threatening conditions (allergic and infective conjunctivitis, blepharitis, dry eye, superficial injury), e.g. ketotifen, olopatadine, acetylcysteine, polymyxin B, atropine and pilocarpine; supplied direct only in an emergency.
examTraps: Thinking eye drops can be GSL.
Forgetting medical device problems are reported to the MHRA too.
Self-prescribing POMs for yourself or family: avoid, except minor ailments or emergencies.

diagram.description: A pyramid or ladder with three medicine categories (GSL at the bottom, P in the middle, POM at the top) and, beside it, the levels of optometric practice: all optometrists, Additional Supply, Supplementary Prescriber, Independent Prescriber, with arrows showing what each can access.

goDeeper.heading: Supplementary prescribing and PGDs
goDeeper.body: Supplementary prescribing is a voluntary partnership with an independent prescriber (a doctor) under a patient-specific clinical management plan, useful for glaucoma and post-surgical care. Patient Group Directions allow co-management (e.g. after surgery) with drugs outside the usual lists; they're signed by a senior doctor and a senior pharmacist.

goDeeper.heading: Instillation by unregistered staff
goDeeper.body: The optometrist stays responsible, must be on the premises and able to intervene. Ignorance of the law is no excuse.

topics.title: Anti-infectives, anti-allergy drugs and anti-inflammatories
topics.summary: Most eye infections and inflammations seen in practice are treated with a handful of drug groups: antibiotics for bacterial infection, antivirals for herpes simplex, anti-allergy drugs for allergic conjunctivitis, and steroids or NSAIDs for inflammation. Knowing when not to treat, and when a steroid could be dangerous, matters as much as knowing what to use.
keyPoints: Most acute bacterial conjunctivitis gets better on its own; a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol may speed recovery when it's severe or not settling.
Contact lens–related keratitis is an emergency because of Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba risk; it's usually managed in hospital with fluoroquinolones or other intensive treatment.
Herpes simplex dendritic ulcers are treated with an antiviral (for example aciclovir or ganciclovir), never with a steroid alone.
Allergic conjunctivitis: mast cell stabilisers (for example sodium cromoglicate) and antihistamines; dual-action drugs (for example olopatadine) do both.
Topical steroids reduce inflammation but can raise IOP, cause cataract and make herpes or fungal infections much worse.
Topical NSAIDs (for example ketorolac, nepafenac) are used for pain and inflammation, especially after cataract surgery.
examTraps: Using a steroid on an undiagnosed red eye: it can turn a herpes ulcer into a sight-threatening one.
Treating a contact lens ulcer as simple conjunctivitis.
Expecting a mast cell stabiliser to work straight away: it takes days and works best before exposure.

diagram.description: A flow chart starting at 'red eye'. Branches: bacterial conjunctivitis → often self-limiting, consider chloramphenicol; viral conjunctivitis → supportive care; allergic → mast cell stabiliser / antihistamine; herpes simplex keratitis → antiviral, refer per protocol; contact lens ulcer → emergency referral; anterior uveitis → urgent referral for steroid and cycloplegic.

goDeeper.heading: Antibiotics
goDeeper.body: Chloramphenicol is broad-spectrum and widely used for superficial infections (drops in the day, ointment at night). Fusidic acid works mainly against staphylococci and is used twice daily. Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are reserved for more serious infections such as keratitis. Overuse drives antibiotic resistance, so treat only when there's a clear benefit.

goDeeper.heading: Steroids
goDeeper.body: Topical steroids range from potent (dexamethasone, prednisolone acetate 1%) to milder or 'soft' (fluorometholone, loteprednol). They're used for uveitis, after surgery and for some severe allergic or immune conditions, usually under specialist care. Risks: raised IOP in 'steroid responders', posterior subcapsular cataract, delayed healing and worsening of infections. They're tapered rather than stopped suddenly after longer courses.

goDeeper.heading: Anti-allergy drugs
goDeeper.body: Mast cell stabilisers (sodium cromoglicate, lodoxamide) stop mast cells releasing histamine, so they are best started before the allergy season and take several days to work. Antihistamines (for example antazoline, azelastine) give quick relief of itch. Dual-action drugs (olopatadine, ketotifen) combine both. Cold compresses and avoiding the allergen help too.

cases.scenario: A 30-year-old has had a sticky, red left eye for two days. No pain, normal vision, no contact lenses. There's a purulent discharge and the cornea is clear.
cases.question: How would you manage this?
cases.modelAnswer: Likely acute bacterial conjunctivitis, which is usually self-limiting. Advise lid hygiene, cleaning discharge, not sharing towels and handwashing. If severe or not improving after a few days, a topical antibiotic such as chloramphenicol can be supplied (within the optometrist's legal scope). Advise returning urgently if pain, photophobia or blurred vision develops.

topics.title: Glaucoma medicines
topics.summary: Glaucoma treatment lowers intraocular pressure, either by reducing aqueous production or by increasing outflow. Prostaglandin analogues are the usual first drop; beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists are added if needed. NICE now recommends laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) as a first-line option for many patients. Optometrists need to know side effects and contraindications to support patients.
keyPoints: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost, tafluprost): increase uveoscleral outflow, once a day at night. Side effects: red eye, longer darker lashes, darker iris, skin around the eye darkening, fat loss around the eye.
Beta-blockers (timolol, betaxolol): reduce aqueous production. Avoid in asthma/COPD, slow heart rate and heart block.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors: drops (dorzolamide, brinzolamide) reduce production; oral acetazolamide is used short-term (tingling, tiredness, kidney stones, low potassium).
Alpha-2 agonists (brimonidine): reduce production and increase outflow; allergy is common; avoid in young children.
NICE NG81 recommends offering selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) as first treatment for ocular hypertension (at the treatment threshold) and chronic open-angle glaucoma.
Adherence is a major problem: forgetting drops, poor technique and side effects all reduce effectiveness.
examTraps: Forgetting that beta-blocker drops can cause asthma attacks or fainting.
Telling patients the iris colour change from prostaglandins will go away: it's usually permanent.
Assuming that once IOP is 'normal' the patient can stop drops.

diagram.description: Cross-section of the anterior eye with labels showing where each drug class acts: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-blockers and alpha-agonists on the ciliary body (reduce production); prostaglandin analogues on the uveoscleral route; pilocarpine and SLT on the trabecular meshwork (increase conventional outflow).

goDeeper.heading: Choosing and adding treatment
goDeeper.body: NICE NG81 recommends offering SLT first for many people with ocular hypertension or COAG; if drops are used, a generic prostaglandin analogue is usually first. If the target IOP isn't reached, treatment is stepped up: another class, a combination drop (fewer bottles helps adherence) or surgery. Preservative-free options are considered for surface problems.

goDeeper.heading: Side effects to watch for
goDeeper.body: Prostaglandin analogues: hyperaemia, eyelash growth, iris darkening (permanent), periorbital skin darkening and fat atrophy, and rarely cystoid macular oedema or uveitis. Beta-blockers: bronchospasm, bradycardia, tiredness, low mood. Brimonidine: allergic follicular conjunctivitis, dry mouth, drowsiness (and serious sedation in infants). Dorzolamide: stinging, bitter taste.

goDeeper.heading: Helping with adherence
goDeeper.body: Ask how patients use their drops and watch them do it. Simplify regimes, link drops to a daily routine (for example brushing teeth), use reminders and drop aids, and explain that glaucoma has no symptoms until late, so stopping drops is risky. Report suspected side effects to the prescriber rather than advising the patient to stop.

cases.scenario: A 68-year-old on latanoprost for two years says one eye now looks browner than the other and his lashes are longer. He wants to stop the drops.
cases.question: How would you respond?
cases.modelAnswer: Explain these are known effects of prostaglandin analogues: the lash growth may reverse if stopped, but iris darkening is usually permanent. Stress that stopping could let glaucoma progress without symptoms. Don't advise him to stop; check adherence and technique, record the findings and let his glaucoma clinician know his concerns so they can discuss alternatives.

topics.title: Ocular side effects of systemic medicines
topics.summary: From the week 12 PaP lecture: some systemic drugs have well-known ocular adverse reactions, and patients taking them often need more frequent checks. Know the key drugs, what they do to the eye and whether it's reversible.
keyPoints: Amiodarone (arrhythmias): corneal microdeposits (common; appear within about 3 months, don't stain with fluorescein, clear 3–7 months after stopping), night glare, optic neuropathy, phototoxicity, possible lens changes.
Vigabatrin (epilepsy): field defects in about 30%, from a month to years after starting, dose-dependent and irreversible, with reduced colour vision, contrast sensitivity and VA.

Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone, hydrocortisone): posterior subcapsular cataract (bilateral, irreversible), raised IOP and glaucomatous change, corneal oedema and thinning, scleral thinning, rarely disc oedema.
Hydroxychloroquine (rheumatoid arthritis, lupus): early corneal deposits; bull's eye maculopathy in 1–2%, so check the perimacular field.
Tamoxifen (breast cancer): retinopathy (1–2%, reversible if caught early), keratopathy, posterior subcapsular cataract.
Vortex keratopathy (verticillata) can come from amiodarone, chloroquine, tamoxifen, chlorpromazine and indometacin.
examTraps: Calling vigabatrin field loss reversible.
Expecting amiodarone deposits to stain with fluorescein.

diagram.description: An outline of the eye with labels pointing to where common drugs act: cornea (amiodarone vortex keratopathy), lens (steroid cataract), angle (topiramate angle closure), iris (tamsulosin floppy iris), retina (hydroxychloroquine maculopathy), optic nerve (ethambutol optic neuropathy).

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: more drugs to know
goDeeper.body: Tamsulosin and similar alpha-blockers cause floppy iris syndrome during cataract surgery; ethambutol can cause optic neuropathy; topiramate can trigger sudden bilateral angle closure with a myopic shift in the first weeks. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists recommends hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening, usually after 5 years of treatment (sooner with risk factors).
